stem: A function f is said to be continuous at a point x = a if and only if which of the following conditions is satisfied?

options.text: f(a) is defined and lim(x -> a) f(x) exists
f(a) is defined, lim(x -> a) f(x) exists, and lim(x -> a) f(x) = f(a)
The left-hand limit at a exists and equals f(a)
The right-hand limit at a exists and equals f(a)

per_option_rationale.rationale: Confuses the condition for the existence of a limit with the condition for continuity; misses the equality lim(x->a) f(x) = f(a) as a required condition.
All three parts are necessary and jointly sufficient: f(a) defined, two-sided limit exists, and limit equals the function value.
Applying only the left-hand limit condition: this is the wrong one-sided criterion; the full two-sided limit must exist and equal f(a).
Applying only the right-hand limit condition: this is also the wrong one-sided criterion; continuity requires both one-sided limits to agree and equal f(a).

explanation: Continuity at a point demands all three conditions: the two-sided limit exists, f(a) is defined, and the limit equals f(a).

explanation_sections.punchline: Continuity at x = a requires three conditions together: f(a) is defined, the two-sided limit exists, and the limit equals f(a).
explanation_sections.approach: State the property: f is continuous at x = a iff (1) f(a) is defined, (2) lim(x->a) f(x) exists meaning left equals right limit, and (3) that limit equals f(a). Contrast with option 1 which omits the equality condition, and options 3 and 4 which each check only one side.
explanation_sections.lesson: All three conditions are jointly necessary; existence of limit and definedness alone do not guarantee continuity.
explanation_sections.timing: 45-55 seconds. Pure recall. The trap is option 1 which lists two of the three conditions but omits the equality.
